slides.title: Classifying Kidney Transplant Rejection from Biopsy RNA
paragraphs: For this personal project, I asked a specific question: once a kidney transplant biopsy has been collected, can its RNA measurements classify the rejection diagnosis recorded for that tissue? I will explain the measurements, compare four models, and show the prediction software.
actions: State the research question, then introduce transplant rejection.
visible_cues: Classifying Kidney Transplant Rejection from Biopsy RNA

slides.title: Transplant rejection and kidney biopsy
paragraphs: A kidney transplant gives a person a donor kidney. The recipient's immune system can recognize it as foreign and attack it. That immune response is rejection.

A kidney biopsy is a small tissue sample collected from the kidney for examination. It can supply two kinds of evidence. A specialist examines thin sections under a microscope for injury and inflammation. Histology means studying tissue this way. Molecular measurements count selected types of RNA, which include messages cells make when genes are active. Those counts provide the inputs to this model.

In this dataset, the recorded diagnoses come from histological assessment. The authors rescored transplant biopsies using Banff 2019 criteria. Those diagnoses provide the answers used to train and evaluate the classifier. The molecular measurements provide its inputs.
Why seek another assessment when the tissue has already been examined? That is the reason for the proposed use on the next slide.
actions: Explain the two forms of evidence beneath the biopsy definition and distinguish the recorded diagnosis from the model inputs.
visible_cues: Rejection: the recipient's immune system attacks the donated kidney.
Kidney biopsy: a small tissue sample collected from the kidney for examination.
Histology: microscopic examination reveals injury and inflammation and supports the recorded diagnosis.
Molecular measurements: counts of selected RNA types provide the model's inputs.

slides.title: Possible Use: Molecular Second Opinion for Ambiguous Biopsies
paragraphs: The possible use is a molecular second opinion for ambiguous biopsies. Sometimes the microscopic findings are borderline or conflict with other clinical evidence. A specialist then needs to weigh the available information.

The first box gives a hypothetical example. A biopsy shows mild inflammation, but the microscopic findings do not clearly establish rejection. That leaves the specialist with an uncertain interpretation of tissue already collected.

Histology shows tissue appearance. RNA messages provide information about gene activity in that tissue. Because they describe different things, a molecular assessment could add useful evidence for specialist review.

For this personal project, I tested how well RNA measurements classified recorded rejection diagnoses and built software to score further specimens. In the second hypothetical box, the RNA pattern receives a high rejection score. In a validated application, that could give the specialist additional evidence when reviewing the uncertain biopsy.
The example illustrates how RNA could supply additional evidence from tissue already collected.
actions: Read the first hypothetical example, explain the project question, then continue the example in the matching box.

slides.title: Evidence for a molecular second opinion
paragraphs: Banff guidance considers validated molecular tests in selected difficult biopsy interpretations. This supports investigating RNA as additional evidence when the microscopic findings leave uncertainty.

Rosales and colleagues used B-HOT, the same fixed panel of RNA measurements used here. Patients who later developed chronic active antibody-mediated rejection had higher initial rejection-related molecular scores as a group, despite lacking that diagnosis on the initial biopsy. Antibody-mediated rejection involves immune proteins called antibodies. That later-outcome finding belongs to their study.

There is also a practical reason to avoid incorrect rejection calls. A rejection diagnosis can lead to medicines that suppress the immune system. If the problem is an infection, extra treatment can weaken the body’s defenses and make the infection worse. This is a reason to examine incorrect flags as well as missed rejection. It does not establish which model makes the best treatment decisions.
My personal project measured agreement with recorded diagnoses. It has not measured changes in care or patient outcomes, and its value in ambiguous biopsies needs direct evaluation.
actions: Explain the two research findings, then the treatment consequence of an incorrect rejection call. Finish with what this project actually measures.

slides.title: What the dataset contains
paragraphs: The public data come in two downloads: a metadata file and an archive containing 1,395 individual count files. I assembled them into the two tables shown here.

The count table has one row per biopsy specimen and a column for each of the 770 RNA counts. The specimen-information table contains the recorded diagnosis and the study group assigned by the authors.
Specimen ID is unique in each table and matches the rows one to one. GSM6510425 is the same specimen in both. This pairs the measurements with the diagnosis used for training and evaluation.

The 1,395 specimens include 1,193 transplant biopsies and 202 native-kidney controls. I included all of them in my comparison. The article reports those control counts, but the public specimen metadata do not identify which no-rejection rows are native kidneys.

The full study does not document separation by patient or referring center between study groups. It reports referrals from several regions, but all specimens were processed at Arkana Laboratories. Geographic breadth does not establish separation by patient or referring center.

slides.title: Outcome: rejection versus no rejection
paragraphs: The public dataset records four diagnoses. Antibody-mediated rejection involves antibodies, proteins made by the immune system. T-cell-mediated rejection involves T cells, a type of immune cell. Mixed rejection includes both processes.

Those three diagnoses all count as rejection. The fourth category, no rejection, includes normal tissue and other kidney diseases. The authors excluded some diagnostic categories rather than assigning them to no rejection. I trained the models to predict these recorded labels.
I also retained the original diagnoses. That let me examine whether the missed cases were concentrated in a particular kind of rejection.

slides.title: The measurements used to build the features
paragraphs: Each specimen has 770 RNA counts, one for each RNA type measured. Each count summarizes signals from that type of RNA. There are two roles for those measurements.
The 758 on the left include human and viral RNA measurements. The counts describe the tissue as a whole. A higher signal can reflect more activity within cells, a different mixture of cells, or both.

The other 12 measure housekeeping RNAs selected to provide a relatively stable reference. I used them to adjust for differences in how much measurable RNA each specimen supplies. The next slide shows that adjustment.

slides.title: Preparing counts for the model
paragraphs: For each of the 758 counts, I used the same four steps. The right side follows IFNG in my public example, starting with its raw count of four.
Add one and take the base-two logarithm. Adding one allows zero counts, and the logarithm compresses the range. For IFNG, log base two of five is about 2.322.
Next, do that same transformation for each of the 12 housekeeping counts and average them. In this specimen, the reference is about 7.900.

Subtract that reference from each transformed count. For IFNG, 2.322 minus 7.900 gives minus 5.578. So the final value describes the target's signal relative to the reference level. The same raw count can produce a different normalized value in a specimen with a different reference. Those 758 normalized values are the model inputs.
actions: Walk down the four numbered steps, using IFNG for the arithmetic.

slides.title: Models compared
paragraphs: Each model produces a score for rejection versus no rejection. The models estimate probabilities, but calibration has not established reliable individual probabilities here. I therefore call the output a model score.
The constant model uses the training rejection fraction for everyone. It shows what happens without RNA measurements.

IFNG encodes interferon gamma, an immune-signalling protein. The study associates it with T-cell-mediated rejection. I used logistic regression with this single normalized measurement as a simple benchmark fixed in my starting recipe. I did not establish IFNG as the best individual predictor.

The all-RNA model also used logistic regression, but combined all 758 normalized measurements using learned weights. Regularization limited those weights to reduce overfitting. CatBoost combined decision trees, allowing more complicated relationships between measurements and diagnoses.

I compared the models on the same specimens and used the same normalization for the RNA models. That let me ask whether combining measurements helped and whether CatBoost improved enough over all-RNA logistic regression to justify its complexity.

slides.title: Choosing a rejection threshold
paragraphs: A threshold turns a model score into a rejection flag. The fractions show what I count. Recall divides the recorded rejection cases detected by all recorded rejection cases. False negatives are the missed cases. Precision divides flags with recorded rejection by all positive flags. False positives are the incorrect flags.

On screening specimens, first retain thresholds with at least 90 percent recall. Among those choices, minimize false positives. Keep the chosen model and threshold together for evaluation. Minimizing false positives here maximizes specificity. It does not mean maximizing precision.
This gives priority to detecting rejection, then reduces incorrect flags. The 90 percent target is an experiment choice. It is not an established clinical requirement or a guarantee on new data.
Threshold selection also does not calibrate scores. The saved threshold appears in the demonstration.
actions: Read each fraction from numerator to denominator, then explain the screening rule and why its 90 percent target is an experiment choice.

Precision = flags with recorded rejection / all positive flags. False positives are incorrect flags.

slides.title: Validation results
paragraphs: Here are the results on the same 345 validation specimens. False negatives are missed cases among the 169 specimens recorded as rejection. False positives are incorrect flags among the 176 recorded as no rejection. The count labels let me compare both errors directly.

The constant model flags every specimen at its fixed threshold of 0.5. It has zero false negatives out of 169 rejection specimens, but 176 false positives out of 176 no-rejection specimens. That shows why finding every rejection case alone does not make a useful classifier.
The IFNG-only logistic regression model has 14 false negatives and 75 false positives. It detects many rejection cases, but also produces many incorrect positive flags.
The all-RNA logistic regression model uses all 758 normalized measurements. It has 33 false negatives and eight false positives. CatBoost has 25 false negatives and also eight false positives.

Compared with IFNG, CatBoost makes 67 fewer false positives but 11 more false negatives. Its validation recall is 85.2 percent, below the 90 percent screening target. The criterion used during development gives a different result in this evaluation group.

If the intended use prioritizes avoiding missed rejection, those additional false negatives matter. I cannot settle the preferred tradeoff from total error counts alone. I would need to know how specialists act on the score and what those actions change.

Compared with logistic regression, CatBoost detects eight more rejection specimens with the same false-positive count. Combining measurements reduces false positives here. The smaller difference between the two models using all measurements needs closer examination before I treat it as a dependable advantage.
actions: State both denominators before comparing the bars. Pause on the IFNG tradeoff, the recall shortfall, and the eight-case difference from logistic regression.

slides.title: Most CatBoost misses were T-cell rejection
paragraphs: The original diagnoses help me examine CatBoost's 25 misses. It missed six of 56 antibody-mediated specimens, 18 of 95 T-cell-mediated specimens, and one of 18 mixed specimens.

T-cell rejection accounts for most misses and is also the largest rejection group. About 19 percent of that group was missed, compared with about 11 percent of the antibody-mediated group. One miss among only 18 mixed specimens gives limited evidence about what to expect elsewhere.

Overall, the model detects 144 of 169 rejection specimens, or 85.2 percent. This is recall, also called sensitivity. On screening, it detected 157 of 174, or 90.2 percent. The validation result is below the 90 percent requirement I used to choose the threshold.

So the screening rule cannot guarantee performance on new specimens. These errors describe disagreements with the recorded diagnoses. Resolving individual disagreements would require review of the tissue and clinical records.

slides.title: The advantage over logistic regression is uncertain
paragraphs: CatBoost detected eight more of the 169 rejection specimens than all-RNA logistic regression: a recall difference of 4.73 percentage points. Both made eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens.

To estimate uncertainty in that recall difference, I used a paired bootstrap. I drew 345 validation specimens with replacement, so a specimen could appear repeatedly. I did this 2,000 times. The fitted models and thresholds stayed fixed, and both models used the same draws.

For each draw, I calculated CatBoost recall minus all-RNA logistic regression recall. The middle 95 percent of those differences, from the 2.5th to the 97.5th percentile, gave an interval of about minus 0.01 to plus 9.74 percentage points. It includes zero, so this comparison did not establish a clear recall advantage.

That bootstrap held training and selection fixed. A particular training and screening split might favor one model. I therefore asked a different question: would changing those specimen assignments change which model the procedure selected? The next slide shows how I checked.
actions: Explain what stayed fixed during the bootstrap, then distinguish uncertainty in the recall difference from sensitivity of model choice to the development split.

slides.title: Model choice depended on the development split
paragraphs: I randomly split the 1,050 discovery specimens 20 times, using fixed seeds to make the assignments reproducible. Each time, I set aside 210 specimens for assessment, then 210 for screening, leaving 630 for fitting. Both steps kept the four diagnosis proportions similar.

Both model families used the same rows and all 758 measurements. Fitting trained each candidate. Screening selected its threshold to retain at least 90 percent recall, then selected by the fewest false flags, using ROC-AUC to break ties. Assessment measured later errors without changing the choice. The 345 author-validation specimens were not used.
The table shows which model screening selected: CatBoost in 13 of the 20 repetitions and all-RNA logistic regression in seven. Changing the development assignments changed the selected family.

These repetitions shared specimens, so they were not independent trials and the counts did not prove a winner. They showed that logistic regression remained a credible simpler option. This follow-up did not change the saved model used in the demonstration.

slides.title: Prediction service and demonstration
paragraphs: I will now turn to the software and demonstration. Training and prediction use the same preparation code. The service reads a CSV, checks the required counts, and normalizes them into 758 model inputs. It then scores those inputs with the saved model.
The command line and the web application both use this code. This matters because a difference in preparation between analysis and the application could change the results.
The response contains specimen ID, model score, threshold, rejection flag, and model version. The version identifies the saved model. The flag records whether the score crossed its threshold.

The service loads the model controlled by this project. The caller supplies the count file. Missing measurements, duplicate names, negative counts, and non-finite values produce an error and stop scoring. The next slide shows both a valid request and a missing-measurement error.

slides.title: Possible next steps
paragraphs: These are ideas for extending my personal project. I compared models against recorded diagnoses in one public dataset. I would want to learn whether those results hold on other transplant biopsies.

One possible extension would test the saved models and thresholds on another dataset, retaining logistic regression as a comparison. Patient and center identifiers would allow checks for overlap, and laboratory quality records would help assess assay consistency. A transplant-only dataset would also avoid mixing in native-kidney controls.

A separate question is whether RNA adds useful evidence when a biopsy is difficult to interpret. Investigating that would require clinical collaborators and examples of the uncertain diagnoses this project has not directly evaluated.

One possible approach would compare specialist assessment with and without the RNA score, using independent review and follow-up outcomes to examine any changes in interpretation or care. These are possible research questions beyond the analysis and demonstration I completed here.

backups.title: Backup: measuring biopsy RNA with NanoString nCounter
paragraphs: RNA includes messages cells make when genes are active. Measuring those messages gives me information about activity in the biopsy tissue.

An assay is a laboratory test. NanoString nCounter is the measurement system used for the public dataset. B-HOT is the panel: the fixed list of RNA types selected for measurement. An assay target means the type of RNA that a probe recognizes.

The laboratory extracts RNA from preserved tissue. Probes recognize selected RNAs, and NanoString nCounter counts their identifying barcodes. Each resulting count is a number associated with a named RNA measurement.
For example, IFNG is one of the measurements. Its raw count is four in the public specimen used in the preparation example and application demonstration.

paragraphs: This table compares the four models on the same 345 validation specimens. Miss counts use the 169 recorded rejection specimens. False-flag counts use the 176 recorded no-rejection specimens. Sensitivity is the fraction of rejection specimens flagged. Specificity is the fraction of no-rejection specimens left unflagged.

CatBoost has 85.2 percent sensitivity and 95.5 percent specificity, compared with 80.5 and 95.5 percent for all-RNA logistic regression. ROC-AUC describes how well the scores rank rejection above no rejection across possible thresholds. CatBoost has ROC-AUC 0.969, logistic regression 0.956, IFNG 0.842, and the constant baseline 0.500. backups.title: Backup: normalization and model settings
paragraphs: For each RNA measurement, add one to the raw count and take its base-two logarithm. Subtract the average of the 12 housekeeping counts after applying the same log transformation. This expresses the measurement relative to the specimen's housekeeping reference. The 758 resulting values are the model inputs.

Logistic regression has one additional preparation step. For each normalized measurement, calculate its average and standard deviation across training specimens. Subtract that average and divide by that standard deviation. Reuse those same training values for screening, validation, and future requests. This puts the measurements on comparable scales. CatBoost does not use that additional scaling step here.

The all-RNA logistic regression uses regularization setting C equal to 0.1. The IFNG-only logistic regression uses C equal to 1. The selected CatBoost model uses 300 trees with depth four and learning rate 0.04. These settings describe the saved comparison.
actions: Use the formula for normalization questions and the training averages for logistic-scaling questions.

paragraphs: This plot groups the 345 validation specimens into ten fixed CatBoost score ranges. Within each range, it compares the average score with the fraction of specimens recorded as rejection. The diagonal shows where the model score and observed fraction would match.

In the highlighted range from 0.8 to 0.9, the mean score is 0.847. Seven of the 16 specimens have recorded rejection, or 43.8 percent. The displayed 95 percent interval for that fraction runs from 23.1 to 66.8 percent. The group is small, and this range was highlighted after inspecting the plot.

A model can rank specimens well while its numerical scores differ from the observed rejection fractions. I did not fit a calibration model on these validation specimens. The application therefore calls its output a model score.

backups.title: Backup: rejection subtype follow-up
paragraphs: This follow-up compared models trained on the four diagnoses with the original model trained on rejection versus no rejection. The table converts each result to the same any-rejection question using rules selected in discovery, so these error counts are comparable.

The original binary CatBoost model misses 25 of 169 rejection specimens with eight false flags among 176 no-rejection specimens. Four-class CatBoost misses 29 with eight false flags. Four-class logistic regression misses 28 with ten false flags. Separate antibody and T-cell component models miss 24 with 15 false flags. That last approach detects one additional rejection specimen while adding seven false flags.
For the separate subtype question, four-class logistic regression correctly identifies ten of 18 mixed diagnoses and makes five false mixed calls among 327 non-mixed specimens.
The follow-up supplied no reason to replace the binary service. Because I had already examined this validation group, the findings need confirmation in a new cohort.

backups.title: Backup: dataset, assay and deployment limits
paragraphs: The full article and supplements do not document the number of unique patients, a rule for repeat biopsies, or allocation that separates patients and referring centers between groups. All specimens were processed at Arkana Laboratories. Specimen-level uncertainty intervals could be too narrow if some observations are related.

The evaluated dataset includes 202 native-kidney controls: 191 in discovery and 11 in validation. The public specimen metadata do not map those controls to individual records, so my current validation counts cannot be presented as a transplant-only evaluation.

The study excluded borderline acute T-cell-mediated rejection, chronic inactive antibody-mediated rejection, and chronic active T-cell-mediated rejection with mild or minimal inflammation, defined as an i score below two. These specific exclusions limit evidence for those difficult categories. They do not establish that every ambiguous biopsy was excluded.

The software checks required measurements and usable numeric counts. The project did not independently repeat laboratory quality checks such as control-probe or imaging checks. Meaningful inputs still require a compatible assay and completed laboratory quality checks.

The score analysis does not establish reliable individual probabilities. The service labels its output a model score. The local research container has been tested, while cloud deployment remains deferred.
actions: Answer the relevant limitation and explain what additional evidence would address it.

backups.title: Backup: sources and contributions
paragraphs: Zhang and colleagues supplied the public study and the GSE212160 deposit. For this personal project, I used their raw measurements for a rejection-versus-no-rejection comparison. It does not reconstruct their published classifier.

The project provides saved model runs, shared preparation and prediction software, and a tested local demonstration. Configurations, input hashes, reports, and source code make the quantitative claims inspectable.

The presentation guide draws on Bourne for audience and rehearsal, Kosslyn and colleagues for presentation flaws, Garner and Alley for connecting statements to evidence, and Rougier and colleagues for clear figures. AI assisted with preparing this presentation.

backups.title: Backup: UNOS research connection
paragraphs: UNOS researchers have studied whether artificial intelligence can identify anatomical issues from donor-kidney photographs. They used historical transplant and refusal records to label the images. Their stated aim includes supporting clinical decisions and making anatomical assessment more consistent.

The connection is the research approach: learn from existing assessments to develop an additional source of evidence for transplant professionals. Here, the inputs are RNA measurements and the question concerns rejection in biopsy tissue.
These are different clinical tasks. The UNOS example provides context for the approach. It does not endorse this project or establish that my classifier improves clinical decisions.
